project.name: opensourcedating
project.tagline: An open-source dating app, piloted in Berlin. One accountable server first, a network of vetted servers later. Chats are end-to-end encrypted.
project.note: Decided means Hendrik decided it. Planned means agreed as a later step but not designed yet. Guess means a working assumption or a recommendation still waiting for a decision.

features.title: Sign-in without passwords
features.summary: Passkeys plus one-time email codes through Ory Kratos (open source). No passwords, no phone number, no custom auth code.

features.title: Profiles
features.summary: Photos, short bio, prompts and intent (dating, friends, long-term). Stored on the pilot server, which reviews profile photos before they are public. Every field is listed in the data-scope doc before it gets a column.

features.title: Discovery
features.summary: Search with filters and browse the results, OkCupid-style. No swiping, no card stack, no one-at-a-time decisions.

features.title: Opening messages
features.summary: Anyone can write one opening message per profile; the recipient's reply starts the conversation. A weekly allowance (starts at 5) limits mass messaging. No swiping and no mutual-like step.

features.title: Encrypted chat
features.summary: End-to-end encrypted with libsignal. The server only relays: it holds a message until it is delivered, then deletes it. A conversation starts once the recipient replies to an opening message.

features.title: Safety and verification
features.summary: Hide, block (silent, both ways, enforced by the server) and report (which always also blocks). Reported users hear about a report only if action is taken, with reasons and a way to appeal.

features.title: Coarse location
features.summary: No GPS. You pick your home tile on a Berlin map with a ~500 m grid and choose how precisely it is shown; changing it is rate-limited. Results show travel time, not distance.

features.title: Open source and portable
features.summary: Public repo, open code, no patents. Anyone can run a server; once stage 2 arrives, vetted servers can join one network.

mockups.title: Search
mockups.note: The design doc leaves list vs. grid open, and specifies a non-empty state for the early pilot -- shown as three options.

mockups.title: Write & save
mockups.note: Updated 11 Oct 2026: the design doc replaced mutual-liking with one opening message per profile, a reply starts the conversation, and a private Save/bookmark list. These mockups replace the earlier mutual-like ones.

mockups.title: Chat
mockups.note: A conversation opens once the recipient replies to an opening message (not a mutual like, which is no longer the model); the safety-controls layout isn't designed yet.

mockups.title: Profile
mockups.note: The design doc describes three distinct profile views (yours, theirs, and the preview card in results) -- none of these are final. The other-person view's actions are Write, Save, Hide, Block and Report, not Like.

architecture.summary: Two stages. The Berlin pilot runs on one server operated by an accountable legal entity, because search, blocking, bans and moderation need someone who can enforce rules and act as the GDPR controller. Later, more servers run by vetted operators can join, so no single party owns the network. The data model and the safety service are built so stage 2 doesn't need a rewrite.

stages.title: Stage 1: one server (Berlin pilot)
stages.summary: Phones talk to a single open-source server in Germany. It holds profiles, the search index (home tiles, never GPS), blocks, bans and the moderation queue. Chats are end-to-end encrypted; the server relays them and deletes each message once it is delivered.

stages.title: Stage 2: a network of vetted servers (later)
stages.summary: Other cities or communities run their own server. Servers join through an allow-list and agree to a shared safety policy and a joint-controller agreement. Each server keeps its own users' profiles and search; servers pass encrypted chat to each other and share a blocklist, so a banned person can't just move to a laxer server.

decisions.why: Search, blocking and moderation need an accountable operator; one shared pool helps the small pilot.
decisions.alternatives: Federation from day one, pure peer-to-peer

decisions.choice: Self-chosen home tile on a ~500 m grid, no GPS, changes rate-limited
decisions.why: Coarse by default, chosen by the user, hard to triangulate.
Better decisions, no dark patterns, no swipe-patent exposure.

decisions.choice: Ory Kratos with passkeys + email codes
decisions.why: No passwords and no custom auth code to get wrong.

decisions.choice: libsignal E2EE + relay that deletes after delivery
decisions.why: Nothing readable or lasting on the server; works when the other phone is offline.
decisions.alternatives: Matrix (keeps history on servers), pure phone-to-phone (no offline delivery, leaks IPs)

decisions.choice: React Native + Expo, libsignal in our own native Kotlin/Swift module
decisions.alternatives: Flutter, Kotlin Multiplatform, fully native Kotlin + Swift
decisions.why: Fastest for one developer on both platforms; every option needs a native libsignal bridge anyway, and that module is reusable and fundable. See docs/design/app-framework.md.

decisions.choice: Berlin e.V., founded before real users join
decisions.why: Someone has to be the GDPR controller and DSA hosting provider.
Cheap, EU-hosted, isolated from other personal services.

decisions.choice: Bans, verification and hash lists in their own service with an API
decisions.why: Lets stage 2 share a blocklist between servers without a rewrite.

decisions.choice: Allow-listed servers under a shared policy
decisions.why: Open federation lets bad actors pick the laxest server; an allow-list keeps a common safety floor.
decisions.alternatives: Open federation, staying on one server

open_questions: Stage 2: how do people on different servers find each other without copying every profile to every server?
Stage 2: which protocol between servers (ActivityPub, Matrix-style, or our own API)?
Stage 2: how does deleting an account reach other servers reliably (GDPR Art. 17(2)), and what must the joint-controller agreement contain?
Who runs the server and pays for it before the e.V. exists?

suggestions.intro: Recommendations from the research so far that still need a decision. Have an idea of your own? Open an issue on GitHub.

items.title: Apply to the Prototype Fund
items.summary: Pays developer time on public-interest open source (up to 47,500 € for one person). Current round closes 30 Nov 2026.

items.title: Apply to NLnet for one component
items.summary: For example the E2EE chat relay or libsignal bindings for React Native/Expo. Deadline 3 Nov 2026, noon CET.

items.title: Found a Berlin e.V. before phase 2
items.summary: No entity needed for the fake-data test; the e.V. becomes the operator before real users join, with an asset lock in its statutes.

items.title: Write down why phase 1 needs no DPO
items.summary: Holds only while phase 1 really uses fake data. A DPIA and an external DPO are needed once real dating data comes in.

items.title: Human security review before any real data
items.summary: Keep the pilot on test data until a person has reviewed the server, the relay and the sign-in setup.

items.title: Invite-only waves, balanced and recruited at events
items.summary: Gate waves so the gender and orientation mix stays balanced; open an area only once new users would see real profiles on day one.

items.title: Age check on the device
items.summary: Self-declared birthdate plus on-device selfie age estimation; accept the EU age-verification app once available. Never store ID scans.

items.title: Contact the Alovoa maintainer
items.summary: Report their encryption issue privately through their SECURITY.md and ask about sharing pieces later.

items.title: Register the name as a trademark
items.summary: German mark at the DPMA (around 290 €) before phase 2; consider an EU mark if stage 2 reaches other countries.
